Empirical Best Linear Unbiased Prediction based on a Fay-Herriot Model.

Source: R/eblup_fh.R
eblup_fh.Rd

This function gives the Empirical Best Linear Unbiased Prediction (EBLUP) or Empirical Best (EB) predictor under normality based on a Fay-Herriot model.

Usage

eblup_fh(
  formula,
  vardir,
  domain = NULL,
  data,
  method = c("REML", "ML"),
  transform = c("none", "log"),
  mse_type = c("analytical", "none"),
  maxiter = 100,
  precision = 1e-04,
  print_result = TRUE,
  self_benchmark = FALSE,
  benchmark_weight = NULL,
  benchmark_target = NULL,
  benchmark_group = NULL
)

Arguments

formula

an object of class formula that contains a description of the model to be fitted.

vardir

sampling variances of the direct estimates: a numeric vector, the name of a column of data, a one-sided formula (e.g. ~vardir) or a gvf_smooth object, whose smoothed variances are then used.

domain

vector, column name or one-sided formula referencing a domain names column in data. If NULL, the domains are numbered consecutively.

data

a data frame or a data frame extension (e.g. a tibble).

method

Fitting method can be chosen between 'ML' and 'REML'.

transform

Character string specifying data transformation for the response: "none" (default) or "log" (Log-Fay-Herriot model). With "log" the estimate is back-transformed as \(\exp(\tilde\mu + \hat g_1/2)\) with \(g_1 = \sigma^2_u(1-\gamma)\) (\(\sigma^2_u/2\) for unsampled domains), i.e. the conditional-mean correction under the log-normal model (cf. Slud & Maiti, 2006); it does not include the additional O(1/m) terms for the estimation of \(\beta\) and \(\sigma^2_u\). The MSE on the original scale is the delta-method approximation \(\hat\theta^2 \cdot mse_{log}\).

mse_type

MSE estimator: "analytical" (default; Prasad-Rao, with the Datta-Lahiri bias correction for ML, as in sae::mseFH()) or "none" (no MSE; mse and rse are NA).

maxiter

maximum number of iterations allowed in the Fisher-scoring algorithm.

precision

convergence tolerance limit for the Fisher-scoring algorithm.

print_result

print coefficient or not, default value is TRUE.

self_benchmark

Logical. If TRUE, fits a self-benchmarking model via the augmented model approach (Wang, Fuller, and Qu, 2008; Rao and Molina, 2015, Sec 10.5.1), ensuring that the weighted aggregate of small area estimates automatically matches the direct survey aggregate or specified benchmark targets without post-hoc adjustment. With transform = "log" that constraint would hold on the log scale only, so instead the back-transformed estimates are ratio-benchmarked on the original scale (exact constraint; MSE scaled by the squared group ratio; the unbenchmarked estimate is kept in eblup_unbenchmarked).

benchmark_weight

Optional vector, column name, or one-sided formula referencing the domain benchmarking weights in data (e.g. population sizes or shares). Defaults to equal weights.

benchmark_target

Optional numeric scalar or named vector specifying fixed aggregate benchmark target(s). If NULL (default), calibrates to the weighted aggregate of the direct estimates.

benchmark_group

Optional vector, column name, or one-sided formula referencing the grouping / stratum column in data (e.g. province) for group-specific self-benchmarking.

Value

The function returns a list with the following objects: estcoef a data frame with the estimated model coefficients (beta), their standard errors (std.error, repeated as stderr_beta for compatibility with fastsae 0.1.0), z-statistics (zvalue) and normal p-values (pvalue), random_effect_var estimated random effect variance, goodness named vector: loglikelihood (the full Gaussian log-likelihood at the estimates, for ML and REML fits alike), AIC and BIC computed from it, as sae does and as in Marhuenda, Morales and Pardo (2014). The restricted (REML) likelihood is not reported: it depends on the covariates through X, so it cannot compare models with different covariates., df_eblup a data frame with one row per domain:

  • domain domain identifier

  • y direct estimate (NA for unsampled domains)

  • eblup estimated results for each area

  • random_effect random effect for each area

  • vardir sampling variance of the direct estimate

  • mse Mean Square Error

  • rse Relative Standard Error (%)

  • eblup_log, mse_log EBLUP and MSE on the log scale (transform = "log")

  • eblup_unbenchmarked the estimate before ratio benchmarking (transform = "log" with self-benchmarking)
    convergence, n_iter whether Fisher scoring converged, and its iterations,
    model, method, transform, mse_type, formula, call, data the settings, the matched call and the data used,
    self_benchmark logical indicating whether self-benchmarking was active,
    benchmark_summary summary table of benchmark calibration (if self-benchmarking).

Details

The Fay-Herriot model is \(y_d = x_d'\beta + u_d + e_d\), with \(u_d \sim N(0, \sigma^2_u)\) and sampling errors \(e_d \sim N(0, \psi_d)\) with known variances \(\psi_d\) (vardir). The EBLUP is \(\hat\theta_d = \hat\gamma_d y_d + (1 - \hat\gamma_d) x_d'\hat\beta\) with \(\hat\gamma_d = \hat\sigma^2_u / (\hat\sigma^2_u + \psi_d)\). Domains whose response is NA are not sampled and get the synthetic estimate \(x_d'\hat\beta\).

The analytical MSE is \(g_1 + g_2 + 2 g_3\) (Prasad and Rao, 1990, for REML as shown by Datta and Lahiri, 2000), minus the bias term of Datta and Lahiri (2000) for ML.

The random effect variance is estimated by (RE)ML and truncated at 0, as in sae. An estimate of 0 makes every EBLUP the synthetic estimate, and the MSE estimates can then understate the error; the function says so with a message. Such estimates are common with few areas or large sampling variances (Li and Lahiri, 2010).

References

  1. Datta, G. S., and Lahiri, P. (2000). A unified measure of uncertainty of estimated best linear unbiased predictors in small area estimation problems. Statistica Sinica, 10(2), 613-627.

  2. Fay, R. E., and Herriot, R. A. (1979). Estimates of income for small places: an application of James-Stein procedures to census data. Journal of the American Statistical Association, 74(366), 269-277.

  3. Li, H., and Lahiri, P. (2010). An adjusted maximum likelihood method for solving small area estimation problems. Journal of Multivariate Analysis, 101(4), 882-892.

  4. Marhuenda, Y., Morales, D., & Pardo, M. C. (2014). Information criteria for Fay-Herriot model selection. Computational Statistics & Data Analysis, 70, 268-280.

  5. Prasad, N. G. N., and Rao, J. N. K. (1990). The estimation of the mean squared error of small-area estimators. Journal of the American Statistical Association, 85(409), 163-171.

  6. Rao, J. N. K., & Molina, I. (2015). Small area estimation. John Wiley & Sons.

  7. Slud, E. V., & Maiti, T. (2006). Mean-squared error estimation in transformed Fay-Herriot models. Journal of the Royal Statistical Society: Series B, 68(2), 239-257.

  8. Wang, J., Fuller, W. A., and Qu, Y. (2008). Small area estimation under a restriction. Survey Methodology, 34(1), 29-36.

See also

eblup_sfh for spatially correlated area effects, hb_area for the hierarchical Bayes counterpart, benchmark_sae.

Examples

library(fastsae)

# Standard Fay-Herriot model
m1 <- eblup_fh(
  y ~ x1 + x2 + x3,
  data = mys,
  vardir = "vardir"
)
#> 
#> ── Fast Small Area Estimation (fastsae) ────────────────────────────────────────
#> Call:
#> eblup_fh(formula = y ~ x1 + x2 + x3, vardir = "vardir", data = mys)
#> 
#> ✔ Convergence: Yes (in 6 iterations)
#> Model: Fay-Herriot (Area-level)
#> Method: REML
#> Random effect variance (sigma2_u): 2.608103 
#>

#>                   beta  std.error     zvalue pvalue

#> x2           0.0555184  0.0614129  0.9040187 0.3660
#> x3           0.0335344  0.0580013  0.5781663 0.5632
#>

#>   domain        y    eblup    vardir random_effect       mse       rse

# Self-benchmarking Fay-Herriot model (the sample sizes n of mys are used only for
# illustration; benchmarking normally weights the areas by population shares)
m1_bench <- eblup_fh(
  y ~ x1 + x2 + x3,
  data = mys,
  vardir = "vardir",
  self_benchmark = TRUE,
  benchmark_weight = "n"
)
